articles.title: Run, Paul, Run
articles.content:
Sen. Rand Paul (R–Ky.) is considering running for president in 2028, and a "Draft Rand Paul" website is now live. Paul has made no secret of the fact that he strongly disagrees with the Trump administration on key foreign and economic policy questions, and believes that there's a lane for a more traditional, limited-government conservative to seek the Republican nomination.
Paul explained his opposition to the party's current trajectory, claiming that both the Iran war and the tariffs have been huge mistakes that cost Republicans the midterms.
The Iran war was a mistake.
The trade war was a mistake.
And reckless deficit financing is a mistake.
I'm not afraid to call these out, because we must stop making these mistakes to get the Republican Party - and our country - back on track.https://t.co/PmQUiYh4tl pic.twitter.com/EdBzfmlLeS
— Rand Paul (@RandPaul) November 24, 2026
This makes Paul fairly unique among GOP presidential contenders. Vice President J.D. Vance, who is all but certain to run for president in his own right, opposes the Iran war—though he is forced to offer tepid defenses of it because of his position—but supports the protectionist trade policies that Paul believes are wrecking the economy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, another likely frontrunner, previously opposed tariffs but has not spoken out against them since President Donald Trump gave him the job; moreover, he is clearly supportive of the Iran war.
Could 2028 be Paul's year? His uneasy relationship with the president might be less of a liability once Trump is clearly finished, and if the midterm results are any indication, voters want a clean break with the administration on trade policy and foreign policy.
Was Alice Huang a spy? That question is central to the debate over whether it was proper for Jensen Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia—an outcome Trump personally helped orchestrate when he informed the microchip company's board that Huang posed no national security risk.
Alice Huang, the Singapore businesswoman with whom Jensen Huang (no relation) had an affair, was "in contact with Chinese intelligence while the affair was ongoing," according to The Wall Street Journal. That makes it sound like an open-and-shut case…but at the same time, the story concludes "there was no smoking-gun intelligence proving she had been actively tasked with collecting information on Jensen Huang or passing along national-security secrets."
Backers of the Nvidia CEO are already branding the notion that he bedded a spy as "Russiagate 2.0," i.e., a false notion propagated by the same mainstream media that once implied Trump was compromised by a Russian government—one actively working with his campaign to get him elected in 2016. Trump himself seemed less than impressed with the brief that Rubio prepared for him, which had warned of complications due to Jensen Huang's proximity to Alice Huang. If you're keeping track, the two figures in the administration most perturbed by this turn of events seem to be Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who faults Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for failing to sanction Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed.
These all sound like fertile grounds for investigation, though Sen. John Kennedy (R–La.) has indicated he fully expects Jensen Huang to plead the Fifth when asked about his affair. In the mean time, Nvidia's board, employees, and investors all seem pleased to welcome him back.
In case you missed it: I was interviewing Kevin O'Leary when the news broke that Jensen Huang had been reinstated, prompting a hilarious reversal from television's Mr. Wonderful.
Kevin O'Leary: Different agencies are going to investigate Nvidia over the next two years. The chance that Jensen Huang comes back during that period is zero.
5 minutes later… "We have some breaking news"
O'Leary: Unprecedented
[The Hill's Rising] pic.twitter.com/Pz3xbEO0Ll
— Clipping Wings (@ClippingWings) November 23, 2026
The CIA disclosed that a recent cyberattack breached the agency, allowing access to unclassified information. From The New York Times:
The intrusion was believed to have been carried out by hackers who used an artificial intelligence hacking tool known as Artex, according to some of the people familiar with the matter. Artex was released earlier this year by a Chinese engineer and has since been linked by cybersecurity researchers to scores of attacks on businesses worldwide, including in Japan and South Korea.
The tool was made publicly available in July and was originally designed to aid organizations with cyberdefense, but it has been adapted by malicious hackers to carry out cyberattacks, according to U.S. officials and security experts.
The breach has many people on edge given the recent technological disruptions throughout the U.S.
Scenes from Washington, D.C.: The city is emptying as people head home for the holiday. I will be flying back to Detroit, Michigan—my hometown—and then driving across the state to Grand Rapids.
The post Run, Paul, Run appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Fifth Circuit Dismisses Lawsuit Over Facebook Removal, Supposedly Connected to Stanford Internet Observatory, of COVID-Related Post
articles.content:
From Hines v. Stamos, decided yesterday by Judges W. Eugene Davis, Leslie Southwick, and Stuart Kyle Duncan:
Jill Hines sued Stanford University, Alex Stamos, and others, alleging they conspired with the government to censor her online speech about COVID-19. The district court dismissed her suit without prejudice for lack of subject-matter and personal jurisdiction. Because Hines has not shown that her injury is fairly traceable to Stanford or Stamos, she lacks standing. We therefore AFFIRM without reaching personal jurisdiction….
This case is closely related to Murthy v. Missouri, which guides our resolution of this appeal. In Murthy, Hines (along with others) sued federal officials and agencies, alleging the government censored her online speech against COVID-19 restrictions in violation of the First Amendment. Here, Hines challenges Defendants' participation in an academic project named the Election Integrity Partnership (EIP). She alleges the EIP and its participants aided the government's scheme to have Facebook suppress her online speech, also in violation of the First Amendment. {Our review is limited to Hines's claims against Stanford and Alex Stamos, the former director of the Stanford Internet Observatory, which was an EIP member.}
Facebook began moderating COVID-19 content early in the pandemic, deleting or demoting posts it deemed false. In April 2020 alone, it labeled roughly 50 million pieces of content. That same month, Hines launched a grassroots campaign to challenge COVID-19 government restrictions and used Facebook to communicate with her supporters. She was aware of Facebook's moderation and took deliberate measures to circumvent it.
The EIP, a consortium of researchers and institutions, was formed in July 2020. It sought to identify misinformation about elections and voting. For about three months in 2020, it monitored elections-related content on social media. EIP participants sometimes recommended actions to social-media platforms and logged their communications when they did. In most instances, the platforms took no detectable action on those recommendations….
To have standing, a "plaintiff must have (1) suffered an injury in fact, (2) that is fairly traceable to the challenged conduct of the defendant, and (3) that is likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision." For the claims before us, the second inquiry—traceability of Hines's past injuries—is "the whole ball game." …
There is one injury that Hines claims is traceable to Defendants: on September 9, 2020, Facebook removed a post from Hines's page that attached an article entitled Masks Don't Work. At the time, Facebook explained the post went "against our Community Standards." It also reduced distribution of Hines's page on COVID-19 restrictions for "repeated" violations of its standards on "Inauthentic Behavior" and for "repeated sharing of false news." Hines does not dispute that these restrictions fit Facebook's own content moderation…
Hines's traceability theory rests on an inference drawn from timing. On September 8, 2020, the EIP received a massive submission of over 200 webpages and social-media posts from the Democratic National Committee. Among those 200 webpages was a single post by Hines where she encouraged her followers to lobby their representatives to end the COVID-19 public-health emergency. In Hines's view, the one-day timing between the DNC's submission and Facebook's moderation of her page is evidence that EIP participants called Facebook's attention to her single post in the 200-webpage DNC submission.
We are not persuaded by her argument. Discovery revealed no communication between the EIP and Facebook about Hines, and Facebook did not remove or moderate the post that the EIP received. {Hines argues there may be evidence of Defendants' communications with Facebook in undiscovered Slack or Zoom messages. But Stanford produced "communications and other documents" mentioning Hines or her account, and Hines neither challenged that production nor moved to compel additional discovery, although the scheduling order allowed for that. The mere possibility of undiscovered communications that were not sought in the district court is not evidence.}
A notation in the EIP's records even says Hines's COVID-19 posts were beyond the scope of the EIP's elections-oriented work. We conclude as a matter of law that timing alone is too attenuated to trace Hines's injury to Defendants.
Murthy also requires us to consider Facebook's own incentives to moderate content. Facebook gave its own reasons for acting when it removed Hines's post and demoted her page, and Hines does not dispute that that moderation aligned with Facebook's COVID-19 policies. We agree with the district court that there's no indication that Facebook, in moderating Hines's post, did anything other than follow its own moderation policy….
I am not at all involved with Stanford's defense of this lawsuit.
Elisabeth S. Theodore, John B. Bellinger, III, R. Stanton Jones, and Stephen K. Wirth (Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer, L.L.P.) and James A. Brown (Liskow & Lewis, A.P.L.C.) represent defendants.
The post Fifth Circuit Dismisses Lawsuit Over Facebook Removal, Supposedly Connected to Stanford Internet Observatory, of COVID-Related Post appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Trump Promised To Undo Biden's Energy Agenda. Instead, He Changed Who Benefits.
articles.content:
The sandy shores of Virginia Beach are idyllic, but what makes the place truly special lies about 27 miles off the coast, at the site of the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project, the largest offshore wind farm under construction in the country.
The project has been more than a decade in the making. In 2013, Dominion Energy secured a leasing agreement with the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management. In 2017, during the first Trump administration, the agency approved Dominion's site plan for the project, and in 2020 its two pilot turbines turned on. But it wasn't until October 2023 that federal regulators gave the final stamp of approval, allowing the rest of the farm to begin construction.
From the shore, it's hard to tell that construction has been underway. Except at certain times at night, the turbines are pretty much impossible to see with the human eye. (If you want to see them from the shore, you have to find the perfect spot and use binoculars.) But if you take a boat ride out to the Outer Continental Shelf, you'll begin to appreciate the scale of the project: 800-foot-tall turbines towering over the open seas like skyscrapers capable of withstanding Category 3 hurricane winds, anchored to the ocean floor with 1,500-ton metal tubes that are 31 feet in diameter.
Despite their industrial appearance, the turbines have been a net positive to the local environment. They serve as artificial reefs for fish and other wildlife, and they have allowed fishermen to continue catching flounder, cobia, and mahi in the Atlantic's deep waters.
When construction is completed—an event scheduled for late 2027—the wind farm will be the largest such project in the country. Its 176 turbines are expected to deliver 9.5 million megawatt-hours of clean energy to the Virginia grid every year. That will be enough to power 660,000 homes, according to Dominion. At this point, the company expects the farm to support 1,100 jobs and generate $200 million in annual economic output for the region.
And one needn't wait until 2027 to see that the project is proving beneficial to the area. Every year during its construction phase, Dominion estimates, the wind farm has supported 900 direct and indirect jobs and generated $143 million in economic output.
But in December 2025, the Interior Department issued a stop-work order for the Coastal Virginia project out of the blue.
What might compel the Trump administration to halt the construction of a project that supported countless jobs and was backed by the first Trump administration? The same rationale that keeps recurring when the president tries to justify his takeover of America's energy markets: "national security."
When President Donald Trump was on the campaign trail in 2024, he promised to unleash America's energy dominance. "We're going to be energy-dominant, we're going to make a fortune, we're going to supply it all over Europe, all over the world," he told Fox News' Maria Bartiromo that August. "We're going to be double and triple what they're doing. We're going to have tremendous energy, and we're going to lower our prices of energy."
Depending on the energy source, Trump's first 22 months back in office have been either "tremendous" or a toil. Fossil fuels are enjoying favorable policies, and their production has reached new heights. Renewable energy projects face government roadblock after government roadblock (in addition to the cancellation of wasteful subsidies).
On Day 1—the same day Trump "temporarily" halted all permitting for offshore wind projects in federal waters—Trump signed an executive order declaring a National Energy Emergency. "The policies of the previous administration have driven our Nation into a national emergency, where a precariously inadequate and intermittent energy supply, and an increasingly unreliable grid, require swift and decisive action," the order read.
The "swift and decisive action" needed to fix such a dire situation? Increasing the government's power and reach. Specifically, the order directed federal agencies to "exercise any lawful emergency authorities available to them" to increase the generation of almost all energy sources—all but wind and solar—through the Defense Production Act (DPA).
The DPA was passed in 1950, a few months after the start of the Korean War, when Congress determined it "needed a mechanism for the president to direct industrial production towards defense needs without full nationalization," says Gabe Arrington, a national security expert and nonresident fellow at the Baker Institute for Public Policy at Rice University.
Once invoked, the DPA gives the president immense power, with nearly no congressional oversight, to meddle with private businesses. He can force private entities to prioritize certain contracts, award loans and loan agreements, and even block corporate mergers with foreign companies.
"We were coming right out of World War II, where we had a full nationalization effort. This was an intermediate step," says Arrington.
Yet the DPA has had a long legacy, and has been invoked at least once by each president since it passed. President Jimmy Carter used the act to fund research into synthetic fuels and to establish the Synthetic Fuels Corporation, which financed research and development into these energy sources from 1980 until Congress shut it down in 1986. President Ronald Reagan used the act to stockpile rare earth minerals for military purposes and to direct steel production.
After 9/11, its "use expanded dramatically," says Arrington, including for "body armor, military vehicles, [and] other military surveillance equipment." During the COVID-19 pandemic, both Trump and President Joe Biden used the DPA to procure billions of dollars' worth of personal protective equipment and medical and testing supplies. Biden then used it to boost production in the clean energy sector.
In April 2025, Trump decided to promote a different set of energy producers. In an executive order, the president declared it "the policy of the United States that coal is essential to our national and economic security." The order also designated coal a "critical mineral," opening up the door for future DPA funding.
With these moves in place, the Trump administration was ready to use the full weight of the federal government to shape the energy sector as it saw fit.
During the first Trump administration, the president signed deregulatory reforms for nuclear energy, modernized federal environmental reviews, and scrapped expensive restrictions on power plants. The market responded to Trump's (mostly) anti-interventionist approach: Inflation-adjusted energy spending fell, renewable energy generation and investments reached new heights, and in 2017 the U.S. became a net exporter of liquefied natural gas—a remarkable feat considering the first export of the fuel from the lower 48 states occurred only a year earlier.
Trump's successor scrapped this hands-off approach.
On Day 1 of his presidency, Joe Biden axed the Keystone Pipeline and paused new oil and gas leasing on federal lands. Then, in 2022, Biden signed his legacy-defining (and ironically named) Inflation Reduction Act into law.
"With this law, the American people won and the special interests lost," Biden said at the bill signing in August 2022. A few months later, climate czar John Kerry predicted the bill would jumpstart "the biggest transformation, economically, since the Industrial Revolution."
That transformation never materialized. Instead, the government shelled out huge sums to the green energy industry.
The Inflation Reduction Act appropriated billions in new spending, $12 billion of which was funneled to the Energy Department's Loan Programs Office. This sum, and the office's $100 billion in new lending authority, was directed to support such projects as a Ford factory in Tennessee (which displaced the area's residents), grid upgrades for California's largest power utility, and a solar facility for a South Korean manufacturer owned by Stellantis (formerly Chrysler).
The law also offered expensive tax credits and subsidies for renewables and green tech. Wealthy homeowners and large corporations claimed the majority of tax credits. Renewable energy production, which reached then-historic highs in 2024, lagged significantly behind fossil fuels.
Meanwhile, grid operators were issuing dire warnings about the status of the power grid. In 2023, PJM Interconnection, the largest grid operator in the country, reported that grid demand—driven by electrification and data centers—was outpacing supply. A year later, the operator warned that "continuing generator retirements and increasing demand" were eroding its energy reserves, which could impact its response to the summer's extreme heat. Trump's Energy Department would later release a report finding that, if power plant retirements continued, blackouts would be 100 times more likely to occur in 2030.
This price crunch, coupled with record spending, prompted conservative policy wonks to demand drastic action. Diana Furchtgott-Roth, then of the conservative Heritage Foundation, wrote in the days leading up to Trump's second inauguration that "America faces a national energy emergency because the Biden administration has created a serious and dangerous energy situation so damaging to ordinary people and our country that it requires immediate action." By taking "immediate action" and declaring a national energy emergency, she wrote, "Trump can ensure that America does not walk down the same yellow brick road of Europe's energy and climate policies."
Enough people agreed that the Biden green agenda was a disaster that Trump reentered office with significant leeway to recreate his first term's lighter-touch approach to energy markets. Instead, he doubled down on Biden's intrusiveness.
For example, in 2026 Trump adopted a novel strategy in his battle against wind projects: Pay them to stop operating. In March, the administration reached a deal with TotalEnergies to shutter two of the company's offshore wind projects in North Carolina and New York. Under the agreement, TotalEnergies was given $928 million—a "dollar-for-dollar" payback from what it spent on procuring its offshore leases—which it then invested in oil and natural gas projects. The company also pledged "not to develop any new offshore wind projects in the United States," according to a government press release.
The Interior Department cited national security concerns when spearheading the deal. It has since brokered four other agreements to pay developers to cancel permitted offshore wind projects and invest in fossil fuel generation. Meanwhile, the Defense Department has stalled approvals for onshore wind farms on private lands under the guise of "national security," the Financial Times reported in May.
Projects like these regularly require approval from the Defense Department to ensure they don't mess with radar systems. If they do, the fix is simple: The developer can negotiate with the Pentagon on a fee to update the radar system. If they don't, the project can move forward. As the Financial Times points out, 50 of the projects facing a shutdown would "probably have been declared risk-free." Meanwhile, 30 had "undergone negotiations, received verbal signoffs and were waiting for written confirmation," making Trump's national security justification all the more thin.
As Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association, told the Financial Times, "The fact the administration is telling private landowners they're not allowed to pursue economic activity and generate value from their property is hard to reconcile with conservative values."
Luckily for developers, a federal judge froze the Pentagon's wind order in August. In November, the Senate passed a sprawling bipartisan permitting reform bill that would, among other things, prohibit the executive branch from rescinding or altering an approved permit or impeding the construction of a previously approved project. Certain conditions—including new information on national security risks—would still allow a federal agency to interfere. But even then, the agency would have to provide advance written warning to justify its actions. At press time, the legislation is in the House of Representatives; the White House says it backs the bill.
The government has also intervened to prop up favored industries, especially coal. In May 2025, citing Trump's national energy emergency order, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered J.H. Campbell—a 1,560 megawatt coal-fired power plant in Michigan that was scheduled to shut down that month—to "temporarily" remain open for the summer. Over a year later, J.H. Campbell is still open. Consumers Energy, the plant's majority owner, is seeking $303 million in cost recovery from ratepayers in the region. In September, a federal court vacated the Energy Department's initial order to keep the power plant open. Despite this ruling, the agency issued a 90-day order in November to keep the plant open through mid-February.
"I think that the reliability and stability of the grid is both an economic concern and there can be national security concerns," such as brownouts and cybersecurity threats, says Nick Loris, president of C3 Solutions, a free market energy think tank. But "it doesn't seem like [J.H. Campbell is] generating that much electricity, so I don't know if it's actually solving a problem."
Loris warns that decisions like these can have "secondary and tertiary effects" on the market and prevent investments into cleaner, cheaper technologies. That's happening in Indiana, where an Energy Department order to keep a retiring coal plant open has made it impossible for one of the units to be replaced by cleaner-burning natural gas.
The Trump administration has kept pumping money into coal. Using its DPA authority, the Energy Department has given $425 million to modernize coal plants, while opening up other funding opportunities for the industry. Thanks to an April order, more DPA funding is incoming for the industry to support its supply chains and extend other coal power plants. Yet exports are down.
Nuclear energy, too, has enjoyed favored status under Trump 2.0, including using the DPA to enrich nuclear fuel. This move has been praised by the industry, which sees America's lack of uranium enrichment—nearly all of America's enriched uranium is imported—as a national security threat. Christo Liebenberg, president of LIS Technologies, a startup that uses laser technology to enrich uranium, argues that the Energy Department's use of the DPA to finance uranium enrichment is "needed because the demand is just so big, and the supply is so small." Liebenberg says that to meet the government's goal of quadrupling nuclear power by 2050, the U.S. will need a 12-fold increase in its domestic enrichment capabilities.
The administration used the same national security rationale to take an ownership stake in Westinghouse last year. In June, the Energy Department unveiled a $17.5 billion loan program to deploy 10 Westinghouse AP1000 reactors. Not coincidentally, per the terms of the ownership agreement, the government will "get a 20% share in any dividends paid out by Westinghouse above a $17.5 billion threshold," according to Bloomberg.
So even when a national security argument may have some truth to it, it can become a slippery slope. "Rather than making an investment that is targeted for a specific national security need," says Loris, "it ends up being more of a balloon payment to industries and companies writ large that really aren't addressing the legitimate national security questions."

The sandy shores of Virginia Beach are idyllic, but what makes the place truly special lies about 27 miles off the coast, at the site of the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project, the largest offshore wind farm under construction in the country.

The project has been more than a decade in the making. In 2013, Dominion Energy secured a leasing agreement with the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management. In 2017, during the first Trump administration, the agency approved Dominion's site plan for the project, and in 2020 its two pilot turbines turned on. But it wasn't until October 2023 that federal regulators gave the final stamp of approval, allowing the rest of the farm to begin construction.

From the shore, it's hard to tell that construction has been underway. Except at certain times at night, the turbines are pretty much impossible to see with the human eye. (If you want to see them from the shore, you have to find the perfect spot and use binoculars.) But if you take a boat ride out to the Outer Continental Shelf, you'll begin to appreciate the scale of the project: 800-foot-tall turbines towering over the open seas like skyscrapers capable of withstanding Category 3 hurricane winds, anchored to the ocean floor with 1,500-ton metal tubes that are 31 feet in diameter.

Despite their industrial appearance, the turbines have been a net positive to the local environment. They serve as artificial reefs for fish and other wildlife, and they have allowed fishermen to continue catching flounder, cobia, and mahi in the Atlantic's deep waters.

When construction is completed—an event scheduled for late 2027—the wind farm will be the largest such project in the country. Its 176 turbines are expected to deliver 9.5 million megawatt-hours of clean energy to the Virginia grid every year. That will be enough to power 660,000 homes, according to Dominion. At this point, the company expects the farm to support 1,100 jobs and generate $200 million in annual economic output for the region.

And one needn't wait until 2027 to see that the project is proving beneficial to the area. Every year during its construction phase, Dominion estimates, the wind farm has supported 900 direct and indirect jobs and generated $143 million in economic output.

But in December 2025, the Interior Department issued a stop-work order for the Coastal Virginia project out of the blue. 

What might compel the Trump administration to halt the construction of a project that supported countless jobs and was backed by the first Trump administration? The same rationale that keeps recurring when the president tries to justify his takeover of America's energy markets: "national security."

Trump's National Energy Emergency and the Defense Production Act

When President Donald Trump was on the campaign trail in 2024, he promised to unleash America's energy dominance. "We're going to be energy-dominant, we're going to make a fortune, we're going to supply it all over Europe, all over the world," he told Fox News' Maria Bartiromo that August. "We're going to be double and triple what they're doing. We're going to have tremendous energy, and we're going to lower our prices of energy."

Depending on the energy source, Trump's first 22 months back in office have been either "tremendous" or a toil. Fossil fuels are enjoying favorable policies, and their production has reached new heights. Renewable energy projects face government roadblock after government roadblock (in addition to the cancellation of wasteful subsidies).

On Day 1—the same day Trump "temporarily" halted all permitting for offshore wind projects in federal waters—Trump signed an executive order declaring a National Energy Emergency. "The policies of the previous administration have driven our Nation into a national emergency, where a precariously inadequate and intermittent energy supply, and an increasingly unreliable grid, require swift and decisive action," the order read. 

The "swift and decisive action" needed to fix such a dire situation? Increasing the government's power and reach. Specifically, the order directed federal agencies to "exercise any lawful emergency authorities available to them" to increase the generation of almost all energy sources—all but wind and solar—through the Defense Production Act (DPA).

The DPA was passed in 1950, a few months after the start of the Korean War, when Congress determined it "needed a mechanism for the president to direct industrial production towards defense needs without full nationalization," says Gabe Arrington, a national security expert and nonresident fellow at the Baker Institute for Public Policy at Rice University.

Once invoked, the DPA gives the president immense power, with nearly no congressional oversight, to meddle with private businesses. He can force private entities to prioritize certain contracts, award loans and loan agreements, and even block corporate mergers with foreign companies.

"We were coming right out of World War II, where we had a full nationalization effort. This was an intermediate step," says Arrington.

Yet the DPA has had a long legacy, and has been invoked at least once by each president since it passed. President Jimmy Carter used the act to fund research into synthetic fuels and to establish the Synthetic Fuels Corporation, which financed research and development into these energy sources from 1980 until Congress shut it down in 1986. President Ronald Reagan used the act to stockpile rare earth minerals for military purposes and to direct steel production.

After 9/11, its "use expanded dramatically," says Arrington, including for "body armor, military vehicles, [and] other military surveillance equipment." During the COVID-19 pandemic, both Trump and President Joe Biden used the DPA to procure billions of dollars' worth of personal protective equipment and medical and testing supplies. Biden then used it to boost production in the clean energy sector.

In April 2025, Trump decided to promote a different set of energy producers. In an executive order, the president declared it "the policy of the United States that coal is essential to our national and economic security." The order also designated coal a "critical mineral," opening up the door for future DPA funding.

With these moves in place, the Trump administration was ready to use the full weight of the federal government to shape the energy sector as it saw fit.

'The American People Won and the Special Interests Lost'

During the first Trump administration, the president signed deregulatory reforms for nuclear energy, modernized federal environmental reviews, and scrapped expensive restrictions on power plants. The market responded to Trump's (mostly) anti-interventionist approach: Inflation-adjusted energy spending fell, renewable energy generation and investments reached new heights, and in 2017 the U.S. became a net exporter of liquefied natural gas—a remarkable feat considering the first export of the fuel from the lower 48 states occurred only a year earlier.

Trump's successor scrapped this hands-off approach.

On Day 1 of his presidency, Joe Biden axed the Keystone Pipeline and paused new oil and gas leasing on federal lands. Then, in 2022, Biden signed his legacy-defining (and ironically named) Inflation Reduction Act into law.

"With this law, the American people won and the special interests lost," Biden said at the bill signing in August 2022. A few months later, climate czar John Kerry predicted the bill would jumpstart "the biggest transformation, economically, since the Industrial Revolution."

That transformation never materialized. Instead, the government shelled out huge sums to the green energy industry.

The Inflation Reduction Act appropriated billions in new spending, $12 billion of which was funneled to the Energy Department's Loan Programs Office. This sum, and the office's $100 billion in new lending authority, was directed to support such projects as a Ford factory in Tennessee (which displaced the area's residents), grid upgrades for California's largest power utility, and a solar facility for a South Korean manufacturer owned by Stellantis (formerly Chrysler).

The law also offered expensive tax credits and subsidies for renewables and green tech. Wealthy homeowners and large corporations claimed the majority of tax credits. Renewable energy production, which reached then-historic highs in 2024, lagged significantly behind fossil fuels.

Meanwhile, grid operators were issuing dire warnings about the status of the power grid. In 2023, PJM Interconnection, the largest grid operator in the country, reported that grid demand—driven by electrification and data centers—was outpacing supply. A year later, the operator warned that "continuing generator retirements and increasing demand" were eroding its energy reserves, which could impact its response to the summer's extreme heat. Trump's Energy Department would later release a report finding that, if power plant retirements continued, blackouts would be 100 times more likely to occur in 2030.

This price crunch, coupled with record spending, prompted conservative policy wonks to demand drastic action. Diana Furchtgott-Roth, then of the conservative Heritage Foundation, wrote in the days leading up to Trump's second inauguration that "America faces a national energy emergency because the Biden administration has created a serious and dangerous energy situation so damaging to ordinary people and our country that it requires immediate action." By taking "immediate action" and declaring a national energy emergency, she wrote, "Trump can ensure that America does not walk down the same yellow brick road of Europe's energy and climate policies."

Trump's National Security Claims Are a Weak Justification To Block Wind and Prop Up Coal

Enough people agreed that the Biden green agenda was a disaster that Trump reentered office with significant leeway to recreate his first term's lighter-touch approach to energy markets. Instead, he doubled down on Biden's intrusiveness.

For example, in 2026 Trump adopted a novel strategy in his battle against wind projects: Pay them to stop operating. In March, the administration reached a deal with TotalEnergies to shutter two of the company's offshore wind projects in North Carolina and New York. Under the agreement, TotalEnergies was given $928 million—a "dollar-for-dollar" payback from what it spent on procuring its offshore leases—which it then invested in oil and natural gas projects. The company also pledged "not to develop any new offshore wind projects in the United States," according to a government press release.

The Interior Department cited national security concerns when spearheading the deal. It has since brokered four other agreements to pay developers to cancel permitted offshore wind projects and invest in fossil fuel generation. Meanwhile, the Defense Department has stalled approvals for onshore wind farms on private lands under the guise of "national security," the Financial Times reported in May.

Projects like these regularly require approval from the Defense Department to ensure they don't mess with radar systems. If they do, the fix is simple: The developer can negotiate with the Pentagon on a fee to update the radar system. If they don't, the project can move forward. As the Financial Times points out, 50 of the projects facing a shutdown would "probably have been declared risk-free." Meanwhile, 30 had "undergone negotiations, received verbal signoffs and were waiting for written confirmation," making Trump's national security justification all the more thin.

As Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association, told the Financial Times, "The fact the administration is telling private landowners they're not allowed to pursue economic activity and generate value from their property is hard to reconcile with conservative values."

Luckily for developers, a federal judge froze the Pentagon's wind order in August. In November, the Senate passed a sprawling bipartisan permitting reform bill that would, among other things, prohibit the executive branch from rescinding or altering an approved permit or impeding the construction of a previously approved project. Certain conditions—including new information on national security risks—would still allow a federal agency to interfere. But even then, the agency would have to provide advance written warning to justify its actions. At press time, the legislation is in the House of Representatives; the White House says it backs the bill.     

The government has also intervened to prop up favored industries, especially coal. In May 2025, citing Trump's national energy emergency order, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered J.H. Campbell—a 1,560 megawatt coal-fired power plant in Michigan that was scheduled to shut down that month—to "temporarily" remain open for the summer. Over a year later, J.H. Campbell is still open. Consumers Energy, the plant's majority owner, is seeking $303 million in cost recovery from ratepayers in the region. In September, a federal court vacated the Energy Department's initial order to keep the power plant open. Despite this ruling, the agency issued a 90-day order in November to keep the plant open through mid-February.

"I think that the reliability and stability of the grid is both an economic concern and there can be national security concerns," such as brownouts and cybersecurity threats, says Nick Loris, president of C3 Solutions, a free market energy think tank. But "it doesn't seem like [J.H. Campbell is] generating that much electricity, so I don't know if it's actually solving a problem."

Loris warns that decisions like these can have "secondary and tertiary effects" on the market and prevent investments into cleaner, cheaper technologies. That's happening in Indiana, where an Energy Department order to keep a retiring coal plant open has made it impossible for one of the units to be replaced by cleaner-burning natural gas.

The Trump administration has kept pumping money into coal. Using its DPA authority, the Energy Department has given $425 million to modernize coal plants, while opening up other funding opportunities for the industry. Thanks to an April order, more DPA funding is incoming for the industry to support its supply chains and extend other coal power plants. Yet exports are down.

Nuclear energy, too, has enjoyed favored status under Trump 2.0, including using the DPA to enrich nuclear fuel. This move has been praised by the industry, which sees America's lack of uranium enrichment—nearly all of America's enriched uranium is imported—as a national security threat. Christo Liebenberg, president of LIS Technologies, a startup that uses laser technology to enrich uranium, argues that the Energy Department's use of the DPA to finance uranium enrichment is "needed because the demand is just so big, and the supply is so small." Liebenberg says that to meet the government's goal of quadrupling nuclear power by 2050, the U.S. will need a 12-fold increase in its domestic enrichment capabilities.

The administration used the same national security rationale to take an ownership stake in Westinghouse last year. In June, the Energy Department unveiled a $17.5 billion loan program to deploy 10 Westinghouse AP1000 reactors. Not coincidentally, per the terms of the ownership agreement, the government will "get a 20% share in any dividends paid out by Westinghouse above a $17.5 billion threshold," according to Bloomberg.

So even when a national security argument may have some truth to it, it can become a slippery slope. "Rather than making an investment that is targeted for a specific national security need," says Loris, "it ends up being more of a balloon payment to industries and companies writ large that really aren't addressing the legitimate national security questions."

This seems to have been the M.O. under the second Trump administration: using seemingly justifiable, though mostly bogus, national security claims to bolster favored companies and industries. Trump is certainly not the first president to do this. But he is doing it even as administration officials such as Wright have identified a better set of fixes to America's energy challenges—namely, deregulation.

Consumers may not immediately feel the negative impacts of Trump's energy socialism, but the continued distortion of energy markets will soon be seen in higher utility bills and steeper power-plant construction costs. They may also be felt politically when President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez halts all oil and gas projects and supercharges solar development with the same "national security" tools that Trump is using now.

What Happened to the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project?

Despite being targeted by the Trump administration, the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project lives on. In January, a federal judge struck down the administration's work stoppage, and later that month a turbine generator was installed. In March, the farm delivered its first power to the grid.

But in August, Dominion reported that the project's cost had risen by nearly $300 million, thanks to Trump's tariffs and to updated turbine installation projections.

Trump came into office promising to reverse Biden's energy policies. But while he may have changed who directly benefits from those policies, he has used many of the same policy levers, which in turn have yielded similarly expensive and harmful outcomes. The U.S. needs more energy, but bogus national security claims are getting in the way.

articles.title: Brickbat: Ride Along
articles.content:
An internal investigation in Buckeye, Arizona, found that two firefighters, former Captain Joe Frazier and Engineer Ryan Clark, subjected fire cadets and civilian ride-along participants to "severe and pervasive" sexual harassment. Witnesses said the firefighters routinely asked young people seeking careers in the fire service about their virginity, sexual preferences, and sexual experiences, and they often made sexually explicit comments. Investigators also found that Frazier allowed a male high school student participating in the ride-along program to spend the night at the fire station at least twice. Frazier had a shirtless photograph of the student saved on his phone, and another firefighter reported finding the student sitting on Frazier's lap while they were on duty. Meanwhile, Clark admitted bringing a gun onto fire department property, frightening fellow firefighters, and he threatened to "take down" employees who reported the misconduct. Both men denied the sexual harassment allegations but eventually left the department. They were each then hired by Lake Havasu City, which said it was not aware of the investigation. Buckeye police concluded that the harassment was widespread, violating department and city policies, but closed the investigation without filing criminal charges.
